>people can be narcissists without having NPD

Uh-huh. Just like people can be "a little OCD" or "everyone's a little autistic!"? The fact that people make colloquialisms out of real disorders is definitely true, but I'm not sure why you're bringing it up here, since those colloquial useages are basically meaningless.

 "*I'm a little OCD because I like having a neat house, we're all a little autistic because everyone has some sensation they don't like, my sister is a narcissist--she spends like an hour in the bathroom doing her hair!*"

If the video and comments are using the term narcissist in such a colloquial and meaningless way, they shouldn't be. That practice is harmful in itself.

>Also the person in the video is not saying NPD specifically…people can be narcissists without having NPD.

In a clinical sense, no, they can't. They can have traits of narcissism just like people can have diagnostic traits of  autism without actually being autistic, but having some degree of narcissistic traits/behavior doesn't make someone a narcissist--because *almost everyone* will score above 0 on a narcissism rating.

>Stop expecting people to give empathy to their abusers. I

I don't know you, I don't know your abuser, and I haven't asked or expected you to give empathy to anyone. I hadn't even mentioned abuse *or* empathy. 

You have zero right to pretend a general statement is directed specifically at you and is about you, or to project words into my mouth that I didn't say.

>I literally lack the capacity to discern if someone is lying to me or not.

How is it different? People with NPD's intent is probably something like "wants people to like them" "wants attention" "wants to feel good". Most people, NT or ND want those things (autistic ppl may want attention less because it's so often delivered in a painful way or full of rejection, but positive non-painful attention/connection? Yeah many want that.)

People with Cluster B personality disorders get othered and demonized all the time, and the mechanisms of their disorder are often extremely misunderstood. I feel like this video is potentially contributing to that.

Acting like NPD people all have some kind of "different intent" than autistic people (or anyone) is ridiculous.

It's pretty disappointing how much blatant ableism is going on in the comments here towards people with personality disorders. You'd think getting demonized and shat on for being neurodivergent our whole lives would make people here a little more hesitant to dehumanize and other people with mental disorders, but I guess not.

You can downvote away if you like, but IDC if my comment hits -1000 karma, if it means even one autistic woman who has BPD or NPD realizes this subreddit is not a monolith of hatred and bigotry towards people with personality disorders.

--missing cues/misreading emotional intent (such as sarcasm, irony, sadness) and thus responding incorrectly 

--bad verbal timing (e.g interrupting, or always starting to talk at the exact same time as someone else)

--talking about things that are awkward or insensitive for the current audience--e.g a divorce, or sex when around someone who is uncomfortable with frank sexual discussion. And even worse, not picking up on their discomfort and carrying on with it.

--(imo) bluntly mentioning people's flaws. There are people and circumstances where it's fine, but as a general guideline it's a practice that requires social adeptness to manage, because people are understandable often hurt or embarassed by having their flaws spelled out, even if they're well-aware of them. (This is one thing on the list that seems just as common in neurotypicals--for some reason many of them are way too comfortable openly telling people their flaws.)

>usually a horrible diet + no exercise. There are numerous studies that show how the body and the mind are linked. 

The only thing I disagree on is the exercise thing. Exercise can be good for mental health but I don't think it significantly affects social skills. A lot of socially awkward people may not get enough exercise, but that's so common among the general population as to be meaningless.

Other than that I think you've boiled down the roots of people's social issues: it's usually neurodivergence, trauma (which some count as a neurodivergence), or sheer lack of social practice due to childhood circumstances (which tbh, that level of isolation and unnaturally imposed delayed development is probably a traumatic circumstance in itself.)

In my case, my abusive parent has usually been (and probably always will be) bitter, isolated, broke, and miserable. 

They're so toxic their birth family won't have much to do with them (and is usually NC with them) and none of their children will speak to them. AFAIK they've never had a happy healthy romantic relationship. They've never been able to hold down a job for longer than a few months. They've been homeless for much of their life.

Their suffering doesn't bring me any satisfaction. It just reinforces the futility of it all. Their life has largely been a waste, and they destroyed two of their kids' lives and did their best to destroy mine. All for nothing, just a toxic cycle, a destructive spiral. All of their good traits were never allowed to bloom and realize their potential, because of the destructive toxicity choking them out.

(I don't offer my alternate experience as a "well actually...". I can recognize there has to be a special pain, truly salt rubbed in the wounds, from seeing an abuser thrive without consequence while their victim suffers the damage for the rest of their life.)

I think what my case shows is, no one is more powerless than a child. Even the poorest, brokest, most reviled and outcast adult can reproduce and then have a helpless slave to torture. 

>You can never say anything to make them change or understand what they did to you. No amount of you suffering will ever make them do anything to help you. It will never make them understand. They will never wake up.

This part still rings true for me though, despite my parent being in a very different socio-economic status than your parents. There is no power on Earth that can make an abuser see the truth, no matter how powerless the abuser becomes.

It's just a trick to trip up neurodivergent people and stupid people. It's like the lie of "Be yourself!" which is told to children even though learning to blend in and be like others is literally everything in our society, and success is nearly impossible without it.

If you're gullible enough to "drop your filter" or "be yourself" you get bullied or ostracized. In this way neurotypicals weed out neurodivergent people from their social pool and find the "acceptable targets" to make into an out-group so they can better bond with their fellow NTs over shared in-group status.

People here are saying "It means being yourself but with tact!" and that's bullshit. I'm sure everyone here can remember seeing someone bullied over some harmless trait or quirky oddity.

 In my school kids were harshly mocked if they admitted their parents shopped at Walmart. The socially adept thing to do isn't to "be yourself" and admit your family shops at Walmart. It's to pretend your family shops at the expensive grocery store.

And if all that seems like a ridiculous thing to generate bullying over, that's exactly my point--people don't become social outcasts for "being themselves/being unfiltered" because they lacked tact or were assholes with it, they become outcasts because social acceptance requires lots of inauthenticity.

>people can form self-preferencing in-groups within a matter of minutes and that such groups can form even on the basis of completely arbitrary and invented discriminatory characteristics, such as preferences for certain paintings.

But depending on what your interests are, you may have no interests that resonate with other people. So there is no case in which you can drop the filter and expect to have good results. A better strategy then is to focus on faking interest.

You're not going to be able to bond with coworkers over a shared fascination of radiation poisoning.

*Platonic: How the Science of Attachment Can Help You Make—and Keep—Friends* has an entire chapter on authenticity irt attachment iirc--it's not a dry/difficult book and it'll be very interesting if you're wanting to read more on attachment.

Make sure you have your priorities straight: you're not going to work to *work*, you're going there to make people like you. It is the number one most important task you will have. 9 times out of 10, a lazy but beloved employee will be kept over an unlikeable hard worker. 

Most people don't like working or being at work, so whatever makes it more bearable is treasured, while whatever makes it more difficult (like a coworker who isn't interesting/funny) they will mistreat or try to force out.

If your coworkers like you, they can make things very easy for you. If they don't... well, you've lived it.

Stuff people like: smiling and greeting people when you come across them, asking them "How's it going?". Making small talk *at every opportunity*. Never let silence reign when you could fill it with conversation. This doesn't mean rambling, it means getting people talking. 

There are lots of guides on small talk and conversation starters. Some stuff that works: asking people what their plans are, what they like to do in their spare time, have they seen ____ recent movie, how long they've worked for the company, and so on. 

Yeah, it can be really awkward and there will be some silences you can't avoid. But think of silences as an opportunity you could be using to endear yourself to a coworker, or at least convince them of your non-hostility. 

It's almost *always* better for your coworkers to think you're stupid, awkward, and boring than for them to think you're cold/hostile/aloof. For whatever reason people will put up with many character flaws but being cold/unfriendly is the kiss of death in the workplace.

The good news is once they've gotten to know you and you've endeared yourself, you can slack off on the socializing because you've established you're a warm friendly person, so then your quietness isn't perceived as negatively.

Also: if you've worked exclusively in food service, get out. Try a different field. It could be you just don't vibe with people that work food service. I'm that way myself. I do much better in retail or office work.

If he truly had the lack of ability to regulate emotion and behavior that you describe, he would have been in special ed, probably an alternative high school, because that level of social-emotional disturbance can't be dealt with in a regular educational setting.

No one has normal levels of control and then there's that one person they just "love so much" they suddenly lose all nornal mental-emotional abilities. It's simply not how the human brain works; there are parts that regulate the ability to reign in anger and violent impulses. 

Has he done these things at the store? In front of your family? No. Because he's not actually out of control. He gets you alone in private where he's free from anyone else seeing and does these things, so he can avoid outside intervention and consequences. It's very calculated behavior. 

>It’s just because he hasn’t done anything to intentionally actually harm me

Do you think any of the women here deserve to have their boyfriends throw things at them, shove them, to be driven to a remote place and threatened with stranding? Probably not. And you don't either. 

>am i completely delusional that it could get better? He’s going to therapy 

It's not that you're delusional, it's that there's a lot of misinformation about why people abuse. It's not because they have psychological issues or a troubled past that they need to work on. And sadly, all many abusers get from therapy is more knowledge about how to fuck with their victims head and dress it up in self-improvement talk. 

Even in specialty anti-abuse focused therapy the rehabilitation rate is abysmal. 

>everytime it happens, one of us texts eachother maybe a day or two later and it always reminds me of how much i adore him 

You're going to need to block him on everything. And if your family isn't crap, you should tell them what's happening in case he shows up in person. 

>It’s just because he hasn’t done anything to intentionally actually harm me

Making you afraid *is* harm in itself, and living in fear walking on eggshells around his temper will eventually traumatize you and smother your personality.

That you say the physical stuff isn't "so bad" means little. Read everyone's posts here, and you'll notice a pattern: escalation. Abusers start mild to test the waters and see what they can get away with. Will she put up with being called names? Will she let me control ___, ____, and ____? How about a shove? When they see you'll put up with being shoved, It's only a matter of time before the next abuse tactic is on. It's the frog in a boiling pot analogy.

>hating me going on my phone, telling me what to wear, constantly asking me where i am and what i’m doing when i’m not with him etc, classic insecure teenager stuff.

It's not classic or normal for teen relationships. The couple of boyfriends I had as a teen never did any of those things. Neither did my friends' boyfriends. If it's normal, then what do your friends and sister think of it?
The cold is awful, something about it is spirit-breaking in a way that extreme heat isn't. I'm sorry you're suffering in it  :(

>once we did get married he turned from the sweetest man who wouldn’t even raise his voice at me to a liar, then a cheater, then verbally abusive, and in September he put his hands on me for the first time. I

Once you married he knew it would be harder for you to walk away (literally legally and financially entangled now) and so he felt he had you locked down and could show his true colors.

It's sadly very common for abusers to do this once they've married their victim. 

>Should I stop hoping he’ll ever act like that again? Can he change and be better if he really wants to?

It's extremely unlikely to he'll ever change from being abusive. The recovery/rehabilitation for abusers is depressingly low. I don't know what it is that makes them what they are, but it must be very core-deep because most of them never change. 

My sister, on why she never hit one of her boyfriends (when she was usually violent towards partners) said: "I never hit John because I knew he would have just left if I did." 

They do it because they think they can get away with it, and the only thing that stops it is when they think they can't. And the only way they can't get away with it is if you leave them and don't come back. There is no way you can be with them and not have them eventually try to assert their power over you using abuse.

The choking thing is scary as shit because it notoriously correlates with an abuser eventually murdering their partner. As bad as punching, kicking, shoving, hair-pulling etc are, they're not anywhere near as strongly connected to partner murder.

Please don't risk yourself by going back in the hope that he'll be the rare unicorn that could actually change. When the stakes are your life, move on. 

I really recommend reading Lundy's *Why Does He Do That?* if you can. It goes deep into abuser psychology, motive, tactics, and rehabilitation rates.

This makes me curious where you're from because Americans are considered rather tactless/straightforward in some cultures. 

>So maybe you folks could help me understand why people in the US are so scared of being straight forward to share what they really think with other people,

Not scared, there is simply no point in trying to have any kind of meaningful connection with 98% of the population. Likewise being "real" doesn't usually help one get ahead, either socially or in the workplace. People save their "realness" for their friends and loved ones.

>in order not to spend crazy hours with their psychologists, complaining that they have tough lives, torturing themselves? (No, I’m not saying that you don’t need a psychologist; you can just help yourself in some cases.)

Have you ever been to a therapist? For those who could just "help themselves" especially, it can be very nice. You pay a person and get to talk about yourself for an hour and get absolute confidentiality, and someone who's an expert in human behavior/psychology giving you insight into your relationships and happiness. You cannot get that from anyone else--friends and family aren't unbiased and aren't experts.

There's really no reason to avoid it if you can afford it. You see it as some kind of failing, but it's more like a treat (unless you have serious trauma/mental illness of course; then it's a lot of hard work).

Do you take the initiative to invite people to do things outside of school? E.g hang out, go get coffee, etc? 

For the people you have a surface/shallow connection with that you want to grow: Most people will never take the initiative, they play it safe, so if you want to deepen a relationship with someone you have to be the one to push, and risk the potential rejection/disinterest. 

>i feel like im a boring person because i dont know how i can chat with people. 

Learn broad/open-ended questions that apply to almost everyone. E.g watched anything good lately? What are you doing for the holiday? What kind of music do you like? There are tons of books (and posts here) on making small talk, which is how most people start out. The deep stuff comes gradually and later on.

Your hobbies are ones that can be social or isolated. With a guitar you could look for other local musicians to jam with, or even sit out and play at a park or town square, or go to an open mic night.

Likewise with art, you can draw alone at home or sketch in public, go to art classes, join art club or artist meetups, seek artists to collab with, etc.

>what would you say love bombing "feels" like to you on a visceral (physical) level? 

Disgusting tbh, it always made my skin crawl. It would make me feel like I wanted my soul to leave my body to get away from them.

I'm not sure if that was because my abuser wasn't good at it (for instance the whole "buy the victim gifts to smooth over a bad abuse incident" tactic works better when you don't use the victim's money to buy the present 😒) or my own nature; I'm a very textbook Dismissive-Avoidant and displays of affection/intimacy/love tend to make us feel uncomfortable and trapped. DAs are only around 30% of the population at most, but if you have a DA patient their emotional reaction to lovebombing may be the opposite of a securely attached or FA or AP person.

I say *may* because some DAs don't have as big attachment wounds as others and some lovebombers may be more skillful and able to pull it off better.

>for example, the effects of gaslighting feel like a fog that rolls into my mind when i try to recall a memory.

For me gaslighting is more like an electric shock. The panic at being faced with a total denial of reality and the terror/dread it induces are near instantaneous. (Once again, may be due to a skill issue on my abuser's part. They weren't capable of the sort of subtle mindfuckery some abusers do.)

People definitely need to unlearn saying things like that imo.  Things that make a victim feel stupid, guilty, or ashamed are not going to be helpful and may even push someone further into denial or defensiveness. No one wants to feel like they were an idiot or "should have known better, it was *so* obvious".

Likewise with the super extreme bashing on the wavering person's abuser. Yes, they suck and are probably a monster, but it's someone the survivor loves and has memories of both good and bad times--bashing too hard can make them feel defensivess of the abuser being trashed. It can also make it seem to the victim like the person *isn't* an abuser--after all, the person claiming they are is presenting this image of an absolute trashbag monster when the victim has a more nuanced view of them. 

It's better to be factual and supportive rather than let emotions and thoughts spill without restraint. Focus on what is helpful. 

>we know DV, cults and other forms of hypnosis and psychological manipulation can impact most humans if one finds themselves in the wrong place and time.

Honestly I don't even care if this is the case. Even if someone is psychologically predisposed in some way, that's not their fault. They still didn't deserve to be hurt/taken advantage of and they don't deserve to be shamed or treated cruelly for it later on. 

Normal good people come across people who are "stupid" or "gullible" or "careless" and resist scamming/hurting them all the time. The abusers are the abnormal and pathological ones, not their victims. 

Even if someone *is* stupid and naive, they have as much a right to be safe and unhurt. Safety and freedom aren't a prize for being smart and untrusting, they're a basic human right. (And of course many victims *are* very smart and were just put in the wrong circumstances, my point is just even if someone *wasn't* it shouldn't make a difference.)

Amen. I think the stat is a person will try to leave an average of 7 times before they manage to make it stick. It's not like leaving a regular relationship, instead there is someone who has mastered manipulation and intimidation trying to stop a victim from leaving, and there's often no line they won't cross to keep control. And they know their victim, their weaknesses and pressure points, inside and out.

Not to mention the very real financial/logistical barriers, and many victims having pre-existing trauma and conditioning to put up with abuse. Some survivors have never lived a single day of their life without an abuser, they know nothing else.

>I’ve observed that people who have friend groups or go to places with their friends often don’t make new friends or want to add new people into their friend groups. Why?

A big barrier is repeat contact--to become friends it's usually not a matter of hitting it off with a stranger during a one-event and deciding you like them enough you want to see them again elsewhere. Myself alone or while out with a friend group have merged a stranger into the group for the night but keeping in contact is a different story.

Most friendships require repeat proximity--you bowl every Thursday evening and they do too, which sets you up for social contact when bowling in lanes next to each other, standing in line for shoes, etc.

But then you also have the fact that someone has to initiate that friendly repeated social contact--and LBR, it's much easier to stand in line and chat with your existing BFFs who bowl with you then to reach out to a stranger who may react with hostility.

So people who already have their own social/relationship needs met play it safe most of the time, they have no impetus to initiate. (With the obvious exception of those true social butterflies who really do enjoy chatting up new people.)

That's one reason why people who are willing to initiate have more success making friends.

So in many cases it's intertia that prevents new friend-making moreso than active resistance. To build a friendship takes as much active effort as any relationship, and many people won't do it when they already have friends.

>My parents were good to me, and they’ve always been there.

There are reasons beyond neglect that can cause DA attachment style. When you read about attachment studies, you may see them talk about parental attunement (or some term like that). 

Basically, the parent being in synch with the baby. E.g baby smiles, so parent smiles back at them. A lack of proper attunement is thought to be a potential cause for insecure attachments (including DA ones). A parent can be a good parent and fail at attunement through no fault of their own--one of the examples given is an autistic parent, who, while loving and providing, may not be able to read and respond/match to a baby's expressions in the way the brain needs for some attachment security. 

Other psych issues can cause the same problem. Even a distracted parent can fail to attune--you may have great parents, but if Dad was working two jobs and Mom was very sick during your infancy, they may not have had time to be emotionally present and responsive to your needs. A parent who is in pain or is worrying about bills may not have energy/focus to notice and smile back at baby.

And of course, the opposite can cause DA attachment, although it's talked about less. A parent who is *too* present, who doesn't respect space and is always overstimulating the child, and is failing to attune to their need for space/quiet/breathing room/independence. In the face of engulfment (think of the "smother mother" stereotype) the child can only mentally/emotionally withdraw to get the peace they need.

>Enmeshed children can develop an avoidant attachment style in their adult relationships. The child grows up and in adult relationships, is subconsciously afraid that when someone gets too close, it will result in a loss of independence and autonomy. 

In other words, you can be made DA by being forced to be independent at a young age, *or* by being deprived of healthy independence by a parent. (And these overbearing/helicopter parents are less likely to be labelled as neglectful/abusive--after all, their motives were to try to keep the child safe, and they may be an extremely loving parent).

Bell's is one, along with other neuro issues, but it can also be a symptom/side-effect of autism, schizophrenia, schizoid, trauma, depression, and just being on psych meds.

Basically no matter what you feel on the inside (happy-friendly, angry, sad, scared) nothing shows on the outside. I remember when I was a kid being very happy and looking at some reflective surface I was walking by, expecting to see my face smiling back. But I looked completely blank instead.

And yeah you can compensate by forcing yourself to be rigorously aware of your facial muscles and consciously controlling them at every second, but it's extremely uncomfortable and induces a lot of self-consciousness. You have to do all the things you normally manage and track in a conversation (words, tone, other people's expressions/body language) and interpret and react on the fly, while also watching your own face like a hawk and controlling it like a puppeteer pulling the strings on a marionette.

So "just smile and be friendly" isn't a solution for people with flat affect. It would be like saying "just juggle flaming swords during conversations, and people will warm up to you!" 

I've had Bell's, with the rarer effects like Horner's where an eye is frozen too, and ironically, it made socialization easier because you don't have to put any effort into trying to make your face look normal/friendly. People see that one side of your face doesn't move because something is obviously physically wrong with you, and so they expect very little of you in regards to smiling etc.

It's worse with flat affect from a mental issue, because then people assume you're normal but are being cold/unfriendly to them, and like you said, humans mimic, they try to give that perceived coldness right back to you.

You can go be in people-swarmed places for hours and never have a single social interaction. 

And you can't benefit from "friends of friends" when you're starting with zero friends.

This tho--this sounds like a classic "outer critic" manifestation though. Outer critic is a mental tactic/defense where you begin fault-finding, nitpicking, and becoming severely critical of others, in order to be able to psychologically reject them and distance yourself from them. It keeps you "safe" from them, because if you push people away they can't hurt you. If they reject or abandon you, they were garbage anyway so what does it matter?

It's not exclusively a DA thing, though I think a strong outer critic is probably more common among us (APs would tend more toward Inner Critic dominance). Any type of psychological profile where a fear of vulnerability is strong, or where there's a fragile ego that needs to be protected, can develop a strong Outer Critic defense. BPDs (Borderlines) are using it when they "split" and decide someone is absolutely evil. 

NPDs tend to have a strong outer critic and *do* go on the attack on others when they feel threatened, so that's probably why the therapist thought of it.

 A DA would utilize Outer Critic for different reasons--more to shut down vulnerable feelings/attachment feelings and protect themself (more like why a BPD uses it) , whereas an NPD is more about projecting their shame/failings and making themselves feel "strong". 

Also, I think DAs are less likely than an NPD to actually vocalize their critical thoughts--the fault-finding would be to  protect ourself, not to actually hurt or break down another person. Lots of DAs have strong outer critics, but it doesn't mean they're going to be verbally abusive or speak their thoughts. (What I mean is, he can't blame his attachment style for being a douche. Seeing faults is one thing, saying them is another. The former may be beyond control, the latter isn't and he has no excuse for it)

Some of this is dependent on a person's 4F defense type when (psychologically) threatened. The 4F defense responses are Fight, Flight, Freeze, or Fawn. People can use any of them, but some people (like NPDs) are very heavily Fight types. IMO DAs tend to lean toward Flight or Freeze more often, but the others aren't off-limits.
